title: USB-C power input (5 V, USB 2.0)
description: A USB-C receptacle for a device that takes 5 V from a USB-C source and uses USB 2.0 data: the two 5.1 kΩ pull-downs on CC1 and CC2, the VBUS, ground and data pins bussed as the Type-C specification requires, and the unused SBU pins left open.

seo.title: USB-C power input reference schematic for KiCad
seo.description: KiCad schematic for a USB-C 5 V power input with USB 2.0 data: 5.1 kΩ CC pull-downs and bussed pins, from the USB Type-C specification. Free download.

sources.title: USB Type-C Cable and Connector Specification, Release 2.0 (August 2019)
sources.note: Page numbers are the PDF's. Requirements are quoted as facts, with page numbers; the circuit is drawn here, not copied.

source.where: Table 3-5, receptacle pin assignments for USB 2.0-only support

parts.note: Any USB-C receptacle with this pinout works: change the footprint to the part you buy. The shell is tied to ground, as is usual.
Rd on CC1. Use 1% or at least 10%: see the checklist.

notes.text: 5.1k from CC1 and from CC2 to ground (pp. 156, 236)
VBUS, ground and both D pairs bussed (p. 69)

checklist.text: A device that takes power from a USB-C port terminates both CC1 and CC2 to ground with pull-down resistors, called Rd. A source recognises the sink by Rd, and the sink knows a source is attached by power appearing on VBUS.

Rd is 5.1 kOhm. A +/-20% resistor works, but with it the sink cannot detect the current the source advertises; a +/-10% resistor can (Table 4-25). Use 1% resistors and you can add current detection later.
Connect all four VBUS pins together and all four ground pins together at the receptacle, on the board. Unused contact locations must be left unconnected.

For USB 2.0 the receptacle has two D+ pins (A6, B6) and two D- pins (A7, B7), because the plug can go in either way. Connect the two D+ pins together and the two D- pins together, as close to the receptacle as possible. The shorting trace should be no longer than 3.5 mm.
Leave SBU1 and SBU2 not connected unless you need them for a specific purpose, such as audio adapter accessory mode.

A USB 2.0-only sink that needs only default power, and does not use USB Power Delivery or accessories, may treat VBUS appearing as the connection. You then get default USB power only; the Type-C specification defers the limits to the USB 2.0 specification.

This block is a sink with Rd only. It does not negotiate: no USB Power Delivery, no 9 V, 12 V or 20 V, and no 1.5 A or 3 A. For those you need a PD controller on CC, and the choice of Rd tolerance and extra circuitry changes.
Add ESD protection on VBUS and the data lines close to the receptacle, and bulk capacitance on VBUS as your regulator's datasheet asks. Neither is in this block; both are common practice.

rules.text: Place the receptacle at the board edge, with its shield tabs through the board. The shell is tied to ground through the through-hole shield pads, joined on the back layer.
Route D+ and D- together, short, and on one layer where you can. Here the two D+ pads are joined north of the pad row and the two D- pads south of it, so neither pair crosses the other.
Keep the two 5.1 k CC resistors close to the receptacle; their ground return runs to the back layer through a via each.
The VBUS bar is a 0.4 mm track for the pads' sake only. Size VBUS copper for the current you draw (0.5 A at 5 V for a default USB device, up to 3 A advertised).
